items.question: How could distinctions like existence and nonexistence arise without ascent to consciousness?
premises: Distinctions such as existence and nonexistence require determination.
Distinctions such as inert and non-inert require determination.
Distinctions such as blue and non-blue require determination.
Determination depends on ascent to consciousness.
items.inference: Without ascent to consciousness, such distinctions cannot be constructed.
items.plain_english: Without rising into consciousness, how could distinctions like existence and nonexistence, inert and non-inert, or blue and non-blue ever be established?

rows.grounds: compound: spoke + Utpalaguru; sandhi fusion in form

items.question: What authoritative teaching supports the claim that such distinctions lack intrinsic difference?
premises: Utpalaguru stated a principle about existent and nonexistent things.
The same principle applies to inert and non-inert things.
The principle denies an intrinsic difference in their own nature.
items.inference: It is ascertained that these opposed classes do not differ by their own intrinsic nature.
items.plain_english: As Utpalaguru said, just as the existent and the nonexistent have no intrinsic difference in their own nature, so too the inert and the non-inert do not; this is firmly established.

rows.grounds: long compound: awareness-fullness + blossoming + emitted + own-other + state

items.question: What follows from consciousness being the basis of all distinctions?
premises: The prior argument denies intrinsic difference apart from consciousness.
Consciousness can release the states of self and other in the fullness of awareness.
Consciousness can animate all things everywhere with blissful beauty.
items.inference: Therefore consciousness is the all-pervading source that emits and animates the states of self and other.
items.plain_english: Therefore, consciousness, in the fullness of its awareness, releases the states of self and other, and everywhere emits an animation of consciousness that is beautiful with bliss.

items.question: Why is the deity called Vāma in this act of manifestation?
premises: The deity has consciousness as its one body.
The deity desires to make the universe its own within the consciousness-self.
This occurs through the emission of its own power of awareness.
items.inference: Because of this self-emitting appropriation of the universe, that deity is called Vāma.
items.plain_english: That God, whose one body is consciousness, desiring to make the universe his own within the self of consciousness by emitting his own power of awareness, is called Vāma.

items.question: Does the bestowal of form to beings contradict the deity's ultimate intent?
premises: By the surge of its own awareness-power, the deity bestows such a form to beings.
This bestowal appears as an outward giving of form.
The ultimate standpoint may differ from this appearance.
items.inference: Although the deity bestows form to beings, the ultimate truth of that act remains to be stated.
items.plain_english: Although, by the surge of his own power of awareness, this deity bestows such a form upon beings, nevertheless, in ultimate truth, the matter stands otherwise.

items.question: Why is the supreme lord called Vāma in the arrangement of difference?
premises: The deity desires to make the withdrawal of beings its own.
To accomplish this, the deity constructs divisions among them.
The name Vāma is applied in the context of this arrangement of difference.
items.inference: Therefore, in the arrangement of difference, this supreme lord is called Vāma because he constructs divisions while intending their reabsorption.
items.plain_english: Desiring to take back these beings into himself, he constructs their divisions; therefore, in the arrangement of difference, this supreme lord is called Vāma.
